entries.definition: The number of learned parameters in a model, commonly used as a rough indicator of model size.
entries.plain: How many learned numbers the model contains.
entries.example: A 7B model has roughly seven billion parameters.
entries.memoryHook: Parameter count = how many learned numbers exist; it is not the same as file size or active compute.

entries.definition: A model architecture where the main network parameters are generally used for every token rather than routing each token through only a subset of experts.
entries.plain: Most of the model participates for every token.
entries.example: A dense 8B model uses its full network for each token, unlike an MoE model that activates selected experts.
entries.memoryHook: Dense = most weights participate each token; MoE = only selected experts do.

entries.definition: A model whose trained weight files are available to download and run, even if the training data, source code, or license is not fully open source.
entries.plain: You can get the model weights and run them yourself.
entries.example: Many locally runnable LLMs publish downloadable weights under licenses with different restrictions.
entries.memoryHook: Open-weight = weights available; open-source = broader source and licensing claim.

entries.definition: Representing model weights, and sometimes other tensors, with fewer bits to reduce memory use and often improve local inference speed at some cost in precision or quality.
entries.plain: Compress the model numerically so it needs less RAM or VRAM.
entries.example: Running a 4-bit quantized model instead of its 16-bit version can greatly reduce memory requirements.
entries.memoryHook: Quantization trades numeric precision for smaller memory footprint and often faster local inference.

entries.definition: The chosen precision or quantization preset for a model, such as 4-bit, 5-bit, or 8-bit; format-specific names may encode additional quantization details.
entries.plain: How aggressively the model is quantized.
entries.example: Q4 usually uses less memory than Q8 but may lose more quality.
entries.memoryHook: Lower-bit quantization usually saves more memory; exact Q4/Q5 suffixes depend on the format/runtime.

entries.definition: A file format widely used by llama.cpp-compatible runtimes to store model weights and metadata, especially quantized models for local inference.
entries.plain: A common local-LLM model file, especially for llama.cpp and quantized models.
entries.example: A model download may offer several GGUF files such as Q4 and Q8 variants.
entries.memoryHook: GGUF = local-runtime-friendly model package, commonly paired with llama.cpp and quantization.

entries.definition: A tensor file format designed for safely and efficiently storing model weights without arbitrary code execution during loading.
entries.plain: A common weight-file format used by many model repositories and frameworks.
entries.example: A model repository may provide several .safetensors shards for its full-precision or quantized weights.
entries.memoryHook: Safetensors stores tensors safely; GGUF is more directly oriented toward llama.cpp-style local inference packaging.

entries.definition: Key-value tensors cached from attention for previously processed tokens so the model does not recompute the entire earlier sequence for every new generated token.
entries.plain: Working memory for the current conversation that makes token-by-token generation practical.
entries.example: Longer context usually increases KV-cache memory usage during inference.
entries.memoryHook: Weights store the model; KV cache stores attention state for the current sequence.

entries.definition: Video Random Access Memory; memory directly available to a discrete GPU for model weights, KV cache, activations, and other inference data.
entries.plain: The GPU's own memory. It often determines how large a model you can run mostly on the GPU.
entries.example: A 12 GB GPU cannot fit every large model entirely in VRAM, so quantization or offloading may be needed.
entries.memoryHook: VRAM = fast memory next to the GPU; fitting more of the model there usually improves local inference speed.

entries.definition: The computer's main memory used by the CPU and operating system; local LLM runtimes can keep model data there when it does not fit in GPU VRAM.
entries.plain: Normal computer memory, separate from VRAM on most discrete-GPU systems.
entries.example: A model may load into 64 GB of system RAM while only selected layers are offloaded to a 12 GB GPU.
entries.memoryHook: System RAM is larger but usually farther from the GPU than VRAM.

entries.definition: A memory architecture where CPU and GPU can access a shared memory pool rather than relying on completely separate system RAM and VRAM pools.
entries.plain: CPU and GPU share the same memory pool.
entries.example: Apple silicon uses unified memory, so a larger portion of total device memory can often be used for local model inference.
entries.memoryHook: Unified memory = one shared pool; discrete GPUs usually have separate VRAM plus system RAM.

entries.definition: The rate at which data can be moved to and from memory; local LLM token generation is often strongly limited by memory bandwidth because model weights must be read repeatedly.
entries.plain: How fast the hardware can feed model data to the processor.
entries.example: Two GPUs with similar compute can have noticeably different LLM generation speeds if their memory bandwidth differs.
entries.memoryHook: For many local LLM workloads, moving weights fast matters as much as raw compute.

entries.definition: Placing some or all model computation and weights on the GPU while leaving the remainder in system memory or on the CPU.
entries.plain: Move as much of the model as practical onto the GPU.
entries.example: A runtime may offload 30 transformer layers to the GPU and keep the remaining layers in system RAM.
entries.memoryHook: More GPU offload usually means faster inference until VRAM becomes the limit.

entries.definition: Running model inference primarily on the CPU rather than a GPU or dedicated accelerator.
entries.plain: The CPU does the LLM work.
entries.example: llama.cpp can run a quantized model entirely on CPU when no compatible GPU is available.
entries.memoryHook: CPU inference is broadly accessible but usually slower than a well-supported GPU path.

entries.definition: The software engine and hardware-specific implementation that executes a model's inference operations.
entries.plain: The runtime machinery that actually runs the model on CPU, GPU, or another accelerator.
entries.example: llama.cpp can use different hardware backends such as CUDA or Metal.
entries.memoryHook: Model file says what to run; inference backend determines how your hardware runs it.

entries.definition: The number of output tokens generated per second during the decode phase, commonly used to describe local LLM generation speed.
entries.plain: How fast the model writes after generation starts.
entries.example: A runtime reporting 40 tok/s is generating roughly forty output tokens each second.
entries.memoryHook: tok/s = sustained writing speed; TTFT = how long until writing begins.

entries.definition: The elapsed time from submitting a prompt until the first generated token becomes available.
entries.plain: How long you wait before the answer starts appearing.
entries.example: A long prompt can have a high TTFT even when subsequent generation runs at a high tok/s rate.
entries.memoryHook: TTFT measures startup wait; tok/s measures ongoing generation speed.

entries.definition: The inference phase that processes the input prompt or existing context before token-by-token output generation begins.
entries.plain: Read and process the prompt before writing the answer.
entries.example: Large prompts increase prefill work and can increase time to first token.
entries.memoryHook: Prefill = read the prompt; decode = generate new tokens.

entries.definition: The autoregressive inference phase where the model generates new output tokens one at a time after prefill.
entries.plain: The model is now writing the answer token by token.
entries.example: Tokens per second usually refers mainly to decode-phase generation speed.
entries.memoryHook: Decode = output generation after the prompt has been processed.

entries.definition: The amount of input or generation work processed together in one operation; larger batches can improve throughput but consume more memory and may change latency.
entries.plain: How much work the runtime groups together at once.
entries.example: Increasing a prompt-processing batch size may speed prefill but require more memory.
entries.memoryHook: Bigger batch can improve throughput, but it costs memory and is not automatically faster for one interactive user.

entries.definition: A neural-network mechanism that lets each token weigh information from other relevant tokens when computing its representation.
entries.plain: The model decides which earlier tokens matter most right now.
entries.example: The KV cache stores key and value tensors produced for attention so past tokens do not need full recomputation during decoding.
entries.memoryHook: Attention chooses what earlier information matters; KV cache stores reusable attention state.

entries.definition: Rotary Position Embedding; a technique used by many transformer models to encode token position information inside attention calculations.
entries.plain: A common way for the model to know token order and relative position.
entries.example: Some runtimes expose RoPE-scaling settings to extend usable context beyond the model's original training configuration.
entries.memoryHook: Attention knows what to look at; RoPE helps it know where tokens are in the sequence.

entries.definition: NVIDIA's GPU computing platform and programming model used by many local inference backends to accelerate LLM workloads on NVIDIA GPUs.
entries.plain: The main software path many local LLM tools use to run efficiently on NVIDIA GPUs.
entries.example: A CUDA-enabled llama.cpp build can offload model layers to an NVIDIA GPU.
entries.memoryHook: CUDA = NVIDIA GPU compute ecosystem; VRAM = the GPU memory it works with.

entries.definition: Apple's graphics and compute API used by local inference software to accelerate LLM workloads on Apple GPUs.
entries.plain: The Apple GPU acceleration path used by many local-model runtimes.
entries.example: llama.cpp can use Metal on Apple silicon for GPU-accelerated inference.
entries.memoryHook: Metal is Apple's GPU compute path; CUDA is NVIDIA's.

entries.definition: An open-source C/C++ inference project focused on efficiently running LLMs locally across CPUs and multiple hardware backends, with strong support for GGUF models.
entries.plain: A core local-LLM inference engine behind many other tools.
entries.example: Run a quantized GGUF model on CPU, CUDA, Metal, or other supported backends.
entries.memoryHook: llama.cpp = low-level local inference engine; many friendlier apps build on or integrate similar runtimes.

entries.definition: A local-model application and service that simplifies downloading, managing, and running models behind a local API and command-line interface.
entries.plain: A convenient model manager and local serving layer.
entries.example: Pull a model, run it locally, and expose it to another application through Ollama's local API.
entries.memoryHook: Ollama = convenient local model management/serving; llama.cpp is a lower-level inference engine.

entries.definition: A desktop application for discovering, downloading, configuring, chatting with, and locally serving compatible language models.
entries.plain: A GUI-oriented local LLM manager and server.
entries.example: Download a quantized model, adjust context and GPU offload settings, then expose an OpenAI-compatible local endpoint.
entries.memoryHook: LM Studio = desktop GUI for local models; Ollama = service/CLI-oriented workflow; llama.cpp = lower-level engine.
